title: Neonatal Ophthalmia (Ophthalmia Neonatorum)
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Neonatal ophthalmia is a conjunctival infection acquired at birth, most commonly from gonorrhoea or chlamydia. Prompt recognition, appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis and treatment prevent corneal ulceration and blindness, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Ophthalmia neonatorum presents within the first month of life as a red, watery or purulent eye. It is a clinical emergency because certain pathogens can rapidly destroy the cornea.
b: Incidence highest in regions with limited prenatal screening
Two main bacterial causes: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis

sections.p: Both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are obligate human pathogens transmitted during passage through an infected birth canal.
b: N. gonorrhoeae: Gram‑negative diplococcus, oxidase‑positive, grows on chocolate agar, highly invasive
C. trachomatis serovars D‑K: Intracellular, requires cell culture or nucleic‑acid amplification

sections.p: The infant’s conjunctiva contacts infected genital secretions during delivery. In‑utero infection is rare.
b: Risk reduced by Caesarean section if mother is known positive

sections.p: Clinical picture differs by pathogen and timing.
b: Gonococcal: onset 0‑5 days, profuse purulent discharge, eyelid swelling, rapid corneal involvement
Chlamydial: onset 5‑14 days, watery or mucopurulent discharge, mild lid edema, may persist weeks

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by simple bedside tests when available.
b: History of maternal STI, delivery mode, timing of symptoms
Examination: conjunctival hyperaemia, discharge character, corneal opacity

t.b: Is the organism Gram‑negative diplococcus? → Positive suggests gonorrhoea; negative does not rule out chlamydia

t.a: Rapid antigen test for N. gonorrhoeae (if available)
t.b: Positive confirms gonococcal infection → start systemic therapy

t.a: Nucleic‑acid amplification test (NAAT) for C. trachomatis
t.b: Positive confirms chlamydial infection → guide oral azithromycin therapy; if unavailable, treat empirically

sections.p: Management combines immediate prophylaxis for all newborns and targeted therapy once the pathogen is identified or strongly suspected.
b: Prophylaxis (within 1 hour of birth): 1 % tetracycline eye ointment or 2.5 % povidone‑iodine drops
Supportive care: eyelid cleaning, topical lubricants, monitor cornea for ulceration

sections.p: Key points examiners love to test.
b: Differentiate timing and discharge type to suspect gonococcus vs chlamydia
Know the first‑line prophylaxis used in low‑resource settings
Understand why systemic therapy is required despite topical treatment

whenToSeekHelp: Severe eyelid edema with systemic signs (fever, lethargy)
Failure of symptoms to improve after 48 hours of appropriate therapy

faq.q: Why is prophylaxis given to all newborns even if the mother tests negative?
faq.a: Maternal screening may miss early infection; prophylaxis prevents rare but devastating gonococcal disease.
It is usually milder, but chronic infection can lead to scarring and visual loss if untreated.

faq.q: What if povidone‑iodine is not available for prophylaxis?
faq.a: Apply 1 % tetracycline ointment; if neither is available, clean the eye with sterile saline and arrange early review.

exam: A newborn presents 3 days after vaginal delivery with a thick yellow discharge and swollen lids – what is your immediate management and why? — Start systemic ceftriaxone and topical antibiotic; gonococcal infection can rapidly destroy the cornea.

How does the timing of symptom onset help you differentiate gonococcal from chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum? — Gonococcal appears within 0‑5 days, chlamydial after 5‑14 days; this guides empirical therapy.

Why is a single dose of azithromycin preferred over erythromycin in low‑resource settings for chlamydial infection? — Azithromycin requires one dose, improves adherence, and has fewer gastrointestinal side‑effects.

A mother with known gonorrhoea delivers by Caesarean section; should the newborn still receive prophylaxis? — Yes, because intra‑uterine exposure can still occur and prophylaxis is standard for all births.

What are the dangers of using only topical antibiotics without systemic therapy in gonococcal ophthalmia? — Systemic spread can continue; topical agents cannot eradicate the organism from the conjunctival sac, risking corneal perforation.
If Gram stain shows Gram‑negative diplococci but NAAT is unavailable, what is your next step? — Treat as gonococcal infection with systemic ceftriaxone while arranging follow‑up.

Describe how you would examine the infant’s eye to assess for early corneal involvement. — Use a handheld torch, look for epithelial defects, stromal haze, or ulceration; note any loss of corneal clarity.

What public‑health measures reduce the incidence of ophthalmia neonatorum in low‑resource hospitals? — Routine maternal STI screening, intrapartum antibiotic treatment, universal newborn prophylaxis, and health‑education on safe delivery practices.
